newsitem.title: USA: Aug US industrial output rise seen not swaying Fed.
newsitem.headline: Aug US industrial output rise seen not swaying Fed.

text.p: A 0.5 percent in August U.S. industrial production, somewhat stronger than economists had forecast, should not push the Federal Reserve closer to or farther away from a tightening move, analysts said.
"For the Fed, this number is enough to keep them nervous but may not be enough to push them definitely to tightening," said Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd.
"It shouldn't shift the debate for the Fed," said Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A.
Kahan said the key question for the markets and the Fed remains whether there is forward momentum in the economy.
"Right now the most important economic report is still last Friday's retail sales report that revealed consumption was fairly sluggish during the summer," said Kahan.
The government said on Friday that retail sales rose only a slight 0.2 percent in August.

"Barring a revision or a big increase in inventories, that would suggest that third-quarter GDP would be in the 2.0- or 2.5-percent range," said Kahan. "Unless consumption revives, the fourth quarter will be sluggish also."

The industrial production data, along with news that capacity utilization -- the portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilities employed in that production -- rose to 83.5 percent, also did not shift the debate for economists who believe Fed policy makers will implement a rate hike at their next policy meeting.

"This doesn't change our view that the odds slightly favor a 25-basis-point tightening move on September 24," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "This is a big productivity gain. Why should the Fed object to productivity gains?"
"It's still a close call but we think that the labor market tighteness will outweigh the recent evidence that the consumer is slowing his spending a bit," said Williams.
Economists said the upward surprise in the industrial production data was in the utilities and mining components.

"The manufacturing component was right in line with expectations -- up 0.3 percent," said Bhagavatula. "The auto assembly rate was down to 12.6 million units from 13.3 in July and 12.4 in June. So you can see that it basically reversed most of that jump in July -- which was as expected."
The manufacturing component of the report, which economists look at most closely, behaved exactly as expected, up 0.3 percent, Williams said.

"But industrial production has now been up five months in a row and has risen at an annual rate of about five percent so far this year. That uptrend is boosting capacity utilization which had trended down sharply in 1995 to near 82.5," said Williams.

"Now it's up to 83.5, the level that prevailed in early 1994 about the time when the Fed began tightening," said Williams. "It's still below 85, which many people think of as the so-called flash-point for inflation pressures. So we're still below that, but we are at the levels where the Fed began tightening last time."
